newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing trial set for opening statement.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing trial set for opening statement.

text.p: After two years of intense investigation and legal wrangling, the trial of Timothy McVeigh for the Oklahoma City bombing finally begins in earnest on Thursday when prosecutors reveal in their opening statement details of their case against the accused killer.

Since the massive explosion that killed 168 people, the case against McVeigh has evolved -- some might say weakened -- as eyewitnesses proved unreliable and the FBI's crime lab has come under criticism for its handling of evidence.

A harsh report by the Justice Department earlier this month citing failings at the FBI lab is expected to provide plenty of fodder for defence attorney Stephen Jones in his efforts to undermine the case against his client, who is accused of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City.
The report said the FBI lab failed to follow proper procedure and drew unjustifiable conclusions in the case.
That the report cast a pall on the prosecution's case worries Marsha Kight, whose daughter Frankie Merrell died in the April 19, 1995, blast.
"There are things that might not be used because somebody didn't do their job right, and it was my daughter's life," Kight tearfully told reporters at the Denver courthouse this week.
Physical evidence against McVeigh, which would have been handled by the FBI lab, is expected to be a pillar of the government's case.

According to widely published reports, prosecutors are expected to introduce handwriting samples, phone records and a fingerprint allegedly linking McVeigh to the rental truck used in the bombing and the purchase of the bomb's ingredients. Traces of explosives were allegedly found on his clothing.
That evidence remains the government's strongest ammunition against McVeigh, said former FBI Deputy Director Weldon Kennedy, who headed the bombing investigation and has since retired.
"Forensic and circumstantial evidence is much better evidence than eyewitness testimony. It's more reliable," he told Reuters from his new office at a private security firm in Memphis, Tennessee.
As to the failings of the FBI, he said, "that's been hyped so far out of proportion ... I can't even put it into words."

Kennedy also dismissed speculation that prosecutors will not use eyewitnesses because, although they may point to McVeigh, they report seeing him with another man, the mysterious John Doe No. 2 who has never been identified or found.
Such speculation holds that prosecutors do not want the jury to ponder the possibility of an uncaptured accomplice nor the defence to suggest the bomb was indeed the work of someone else.
Not so, said Kennedy. Eyewitnesses who surfaced early on simply didn't hold up or contradicted each other, he said.
While pretrial hearings indicate prosecutors will not offer an eyewitness placing McVeigh at the scene of the blast, they don't need one to prove their case, he noted.
McVeigh faces federal charges of conspiracy and eight counts of murder for the federal law enforcement agents killed. His co-defendant, Terry Nichols, will be tried separately.
Oklahoma prosecutors say they plan to file 160 state murder charges against McVeigh after his federal trial ends.

Many of the 168 who died were government workers or people checking on Social Security benefits. Nineteen of the dead were children, a number of whom had just been dropped off at the building's second-floor day care centre.

Authorities have said McVeigh set off the bomb in retaliation for the deadly FBI raid at the Branch Davidian complex in Waco, Texas, two years earlier, and that he was inspired by the extremist novel "The Turner Diaries."

Powerful evidence is expected from his former Army buddy Michael Fortier, who said McVeigh told him about the bombing. Under a plea bargain, Fortier has admitted to knowing about the plot and not warning authorities.
As many as 400 witnesses could be called to testify in the trial, which is expected to last several months.
